Title: The Stop That Doesn't Eat Your Wheels: The Stepping Plough
Description: Tired of replacing wheels worn flat by T-stops? The stepping plough is a certified coach's favourite non-emergency stop, and it causes zero wheel wear: instead of dragging a skate, you turn your toes in progressively — a subtle angle first, more as you slow — and reposition your feet step by step until you stop. It also chains with a plough or a T-stop for downhill speed control. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Stepping Plough Mistake: Your Feet Drift Until Your Skates Collide
Description: The most common stepping plough fault is stepping up and down on the spot. Each step lets your feet migrate inward until your skates clip each other mid-stop. The fix is deliberate: every time you pick up a foot, lift it up AND out to the side, so your stance stays wide and stable all the way to a full stop. Toes in, heels pushing out, and the base never narrows. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Downhill Combo: A Gentle T-Stop, Then a Stepping Plough
Description: No single stop handles a real hill on its own. A certified coach's combination: scrub off the high speed with a gentle T-stop first, then switch to a stepping plough to bring yourself to a smooth, wheel-saving final stop. Or open with a wide regular plough to shed the initial speed and transition straight into stepping. Each stop does the part it is good at. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: The T-Stop Is a Slow-Down, Not an Emergency Stop
Description: I stop in a T myself, and I'll pass this on anyway: a certified coach calls the T-stop an intermediate deceleration method, not an emergency stop — and most beginners rely on it alone. Without a heel brake, you need more than one way to stop. Her pick is the stepping plough: faster deceleration, a true full stop, endless combinations, even with the T-stop. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby; note from me, Cass, a non-professional street skater. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Inline Skating Stops: No Single Stop Works Everywhere, Build a Tool Belt
Description: No one stop covers wet ground, a narrow path and real speed. Linear stops — heel brake, T-stop — suit tight spaces; rotational stops (soul slide) let you steer away from a hazard while braking. A certified coach's order: heel brake, plough and stepping plough, T-stop, turn and lunge stops, soul slide. She starts beginners on the heel brake; I took mine off once comfortable. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby; note from me, Cass, a non-professional street skater. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Heel Stop 2: Flip Your Back Skate Onto Its Toe Wheel
Description: A certified coach's heel brake variation: from the normal heel brake position, flip your back skate up onto its front toe wheel and stay steady by pointing that foot inward. Practise the toe roll first. She says the heel brake works on hills sooner than any other stop; mine wasn't powerful enough for a real stop and hurt my shin, so I take it off. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby; account from me, Cass, a non-professional street skater. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Your Weak Leg Needs 100% of Your Weight, Not a Bit More
Description: Comfortable on one leg and wobbly on the other? That's normal — most skaters load their dominant leg. The fix is a scooting drill: your weak leg is the only support leg, deep knee bend, and your dominant leg does nothing but push. Your weak side carries all your weight while holding a centre edge, neither rolling in nor out. Then skate in a scissor stance with the weak foot leading. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Film Yourself From the Side: The Only View That Sees a Bent Waist
Description: Skating for hours with the wrong posture only trains the wrong posture in. A certified coach's check: have a friend film you from a side angle — or rest your phone against a water bottle — and compare your shoulder-to-hip line with a correct demonstration. From the front you can't see a torso hinged at the waist; from the side it's obvious. Fix it before it becomes muscle memory. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby.
